procedural_history.originating_court: Presidency Magistrate, Esplanade Courts, Bombay (Criminal Case No. 42/CW of 1962)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Bombay High Court dated 9 August, 1968, 17 December, 1969 and 6 March, 1967.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Bombay High Court ordered the issue of a commission to examine witnesses in West Germany. The Bombay High Court granted the prosecution time first up to 31 May, 1970 and then up to 31 August, 1970 for the return of the Commission. The third extension of time by the Bombay High Court was up to 16 September 1970. The Bombay High Court cancelled Mithani's bail on 6 March, 1967.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Mithani filed a petition for special leave to appeal against the order of the Bombay High Court dated 6 March, 1967 cancelling the bail. Mithani obtained special leave and the appeal was dismissed on 4 May, 1967, but the Court gave the prosecution time to examine German witnesses. The prosecution filed a petition for special leave to appeal against the order of the Bombay High Court dated 9 August, 1968. The prosecution withdrew the special leave petition. Mithani obtained special leave to appeal against the judgment and order of the Bombay High Court dated 17 December, 1969, limited to the question of non-allowance of air fare and daily expenses of Mithani's lawyer. The prosecution came to the Supreme Court for appeal by special leave. While the appeal was pending and thereafter, the Supreme Court extended the time for return of the Commission. The State asked for an extension of time upto 31 March, 1972 for the return of the Commission.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court has the power to extend the time for the return of a commission after the appeal in the case has been disposed of.

facts: The Supreme Court had previously disposed of an appeal concerning the payment of counsel's expenses for a commission to examine witnesses in West Germany.
While that appeal was pending and after it was disposed of, the Court had granted several extensions of time for the return of the commission.
The State (prosecution) applied for another extension of time after the appeal had been concluded.
The opposing party contended that because the appeal was disposed of, the Court was now powerless to make any further orders in the matter.
law: The Supreme Court has the power to make orders that are supplemental to and in continuation of directions it gave when originally disposing of a case.
application: The Court rejected the argument that it was powerless, calling the contention "unsound."
It reasoned that when it disposed of the original appeal, it gave specific directions for the return of the commission, including setting a time limit.
Therefore, any subsequent request for an extension of that time is not a new matter but is considered "supplemental to and in continuation of the time fixed by this Court."
Because the request is directly related to and a continuation of its own prior order, the Court has the authority to modify it.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that it did have the power to extend the time for the return of the commission even after the appeal was disposed of. It stated there was "no impediment" to passing such an order, as it was merely supplemental to the directions given in its original judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether a further extension of time should be granted to the State for the return of the commission for the examination of witnesses in West Germany.

facts: The State had previously been granted several extensions of time to have witnesses examined in West Germany and have the commission returned.
The State failed to get the commission returned within the previously extended deadlines and was now asking for another extension.
The case involved a criminal prosecution under the Imports and Exports Control Act, 1947.
law: Sections 504 and 505A of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) govern the process of issuing commissions to examine witnesses in foreign countries.
These sections require a formal "reciprocal arrangement" between the Government of India and the foreign country's government.
A court will only order the examination of witnesses by commission if it is satisfied that the commission will be "effectively enforceable."
application: The Court found that there was no completed reciprocal arrangement between India and the Federal Republic of West Germany for the examination of witnesses in criminal cases.
Evidence, including government notes and communications, showed that negotiations for such an arrangement were still ongoing and a formal agreement had not yet been entered into.
A prior government notification regarding this process had been issued only in anticipation of an arrangement, not based on an existing one.
Without the required reciprocal arrangement under ss. 504 and 505A, the legal foundation for enforcing the commission in West Germany was missing.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the request for a further extension of time because the fundamental legal prerequisite—a formal reciprocal arrangement between India and West Germany for examining witnesses—did not exist. Since the commission was not legally enforceable, the Court was unwilling to grant more time for a process that had no proper legal basis to succeed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court has the power to extend the time for the return of a commission after the appeal in the case has been disposed of.
appellant_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the appellant's arguments on this issue. However, the court's decision aligns with the position that it does have the power, which would be contrary to the respondent's argument.
respondent_arguments: The Solicitor General, on behalf of the State, suggested that after the appeal has been disposed of by the Supreme Court, no further order could be made.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a further extension of time should be granted to the State for the return of the commission for the examination of witnesses in West Germany.
appellant_arguments: The text implies the appellant argued that an extension should not be granted because it would be an order made in vain, as there were no reciprocal arrangements for the execution of the commission under sections 504 and 508A of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
respondent_arguments: The State requested a further extension of time for the return of the commission to examine witnesses in West Germany.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Supreme Court has the power to make supplemental orders, such as extending the time for the return of a commission, even after an appeal has been disposed of. However, an order for a commission will not be made when it appears that the necessary reciprocal arrangements under sections 504 and 508A of the Code of Criminal Procedure do not exist.
obiter: The courts do not make orders in vain.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Although the Supreme Court possesses the power to extend the time for the return of a commission even after an appeal has been disposed of, as such an extension is supplemental to its original directions, it will not grant a further extension in this case. The court will not issue an order for the examination of witnesses on commission unless it is satisfied of the effective enforceability of that commission. Because there is no reciprocal arrangement between India and West Germany for the examination of witnesses under sections 504 and 508A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, any order for extension would be an order made in vain.
legal_tests_applied: The court passes an order for examination of witnesses in Commission when the court is satisfied 'not only about the necessity Of such evidence but also about the effective enforceability of Commission for examination of witnesses.'

An extension of time for a commission is considered 'supplemental to and in con1inuation of' the time previously fixed by the Court, and thus within the Court's power to grant even after the main appeal is disposed of.
why_appellant_lost: The State's (respondent's) argument that the Court was powerless to make any order after the appeal was disposed of was rejected as 'unsound,' because any extension would be supplemental to the Court's original directions.

The State's (respondent's) application for an extension was dismissed because it could not demonstrate that the commission would be effectively enforceable, as there was 'no reciprocal arrangement .between the Government of India and the Government of the Federal Republic of West Germany for el"amination of witnesses' as contemplated by the Code of Criminal Procedure.
why_respondent_won: The appellant's position prevailed because the court agreed that without reciprocal arrangements under sections 504 and 508A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the commission was not effectively enforceable.

The court accepted the underlying premise of the appellant's argument that it should not issue an order that would be in vain, and found that granting an extension for an unenforceable commission would be such an order.
policy_considerations: The courts do not make orders in vain.
